new_statements.quote: Increased intensity in Laari is most commonly manifested on the initial syllable of the word, without regard to the number of syllables in the word. Increased intensity appears in the word-initial syllable in 59% of phonological words. The next largest number of words demonstrates stress on the second syllable, and the smallest number of words shows stress on the third or further syllables. [...] The increased intensity observed in Laari emerges most often on the first syllable, but this is only a small majority of cases. It does not seem to relate to length or tone. There are no instances in which intensity causes a contrast; no two words are distinguished solely by their stress pattern. Therefore, it seems that stress does not exist in Laari as a significant phonological entity.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Laari is a two-tone (H/L) language; the source finds no phonological word stress. Phonetically, heightened intensity falls on the word-initial syllable in a small majority (59%) of words regardless of word length, otherwise mostly on the second syllable; it is not weight-sensitive, not tied to tone, and never contrastive. Jacquot's 1971 reference grammar likewise treats tone as the only prosodic distinctive feature and never mentions stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Intensity on the 2nd syllable is the next most frequent pattern and on the 3rd or later syllable the least; when non-initial it 'often' but not overwhelmingly sits on a H-toned syllable; no phonological motivation for the shift was found; author says the area 'should be studied further along with moraic structure' (p. 186).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological words (nouns and verbs) from a wordlist elicited in Brazzaville in 2010 from Laari speakers who are also fluent in French; 765 tokens measured (383 two-syllable, 315 three-syllable, 59 four-syllable, 8 five-syllable). Author notes French intonation (phrase-final falling pitch) may affect the data. Jacquot 1971 §1.51 (pp. 57-58): 'des traits prosodiques.. y ont également une fonction distinctive. Ils appartiennent à la catégorie du ton' — tone only, two registers.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the Laari/Laadi of Brazzaville and the Pool region (Republic of Congo): Unseth's 2010 data are from Brazzaville speakers; Jacquot's 'laadi' is the same Brazzaville/Pool variety (Kongo H16f). Same glottocode laar1238; no dialect distinction at issue.

sources.locator: §4.4.1 'Intensity and stress', pp. 104-105 (PDF pp. 124-125); confirmed in §6.3 p. 185 ('no phonological stress') and §6.4.2 p. 186
sources.note: §4.4.1 'Intensity and stress' (pp. 103-105): increased intensity falls on the word-initial syllable in 59% of phonological words (765 tokens), next most often on the 2nd syllable; not attracted to heavy syllables, not correlated with tone; never contrastive; 'it seems that stress does not exist in Laari as a significant phonological entity'; summary p. 185: 'eight syllable types in Laari and no phonological stress'. Two-tone (H/L) language, TBU = syllable.

sources.note: Ch. III 'Emprunts lexicaux intégrés', pp. 56-57: loanwords 'ne se distinguent en rien, prosodiquement, des autres substantifs'; their tone-class membership is diachronically 'le résultat.. d'une adaptation à ce système.. de l'accentuation du terme original' for loans from non-African languages. Nothing on native word stress; vowel length treated as a later development possibly linked to 'l'accent et/ou le ton' (p. 226, speculative).

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Part I, ch. I, §II 'Prosodie' §1.51-1.54, pp. 57-60: the only prosodic distinctive features 'appartiennent à la catégorie du ton'; two registers, haut/bas, borne by moras (short V = 1 mora, long V = 2, m/n can bear tone). No mention of stress / accent d'intensité anywhere in the grammar (a full-text search for stress/accent, 'intensit' empty apart from 'accent aigu/grave' as tone diacritics).
